summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would change the Fair Entitlements Guarantee Act 2012, which helps eligible workers get unpaid wages and other entitlements when their employer goes bankrupt or into liquidation.

It would align the maximum redundancy pay under the scheme with the cap set by the National Employment Standards in the Fair Work Act, and make several technical clarifications to how the scheme operates.
The changes would start on 1 January 2015 or the day after Royal Assent, whichever is later, except for the funding arrangement for legal costs, which would apply from 1 July 2015.
changes: It would align the maximum redundancy pay entitlement with the National Employment Standards cap.
It would clarify that a claimant's initial entitlement is calculated without amounts withheld by law, such as tax.
It would establish a funding source for certain legal costs for Administrative Appeals Tribunal reviews.
It would clarify that a person's death does not stop eligibility, allowing next of kin or estate to claim.
It would allow debts owed by a claimant to be offset proportionally against other entitlements.
It would remove the requirement to take reasonable steps to recover pre-insolvency debts, letting the Secretary reduce entitlements instead.
summary.affected: Eligible employees who lose their job due to employer liquidation or bankruptcy, their next of kin or estates, and the Department handling claims.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Introduced the Fair Entitlements Guarantee Amendment Bill 2014, noting the scheme succeeded GEERS, introduced by the Howard government in 2001, and that costs had grown unsustainably from 8,626 claimants paid $72.97 million in 2006-07 to 16,019 claimants paid $261.65 million in 2012-13, prompting a reinstated 16-week redundancy cap from 1 January 2015.

speeches.speaker: Angus Taylor
speeches.brief: Defended the Fair Entitlements Guarantee Amendment Bill 2014, which caps redundancy payments at 16 weeks to save almost $80 million over the forward estimates, said scheme claims had grown from 8,626 claimants paid $73 million in 2006-07 to 16,019 claimants paid $262 million in 2012-13, and said the change would affect only 2,446 of 41,393 claimants over three years.

speeches.speaker: Chris Hayes
speeches.brief: Opposed the Fair Entitlements Guarantee Amendment Bill 2014, said capping payments at 16 weeks and switching to average weekly earnings would hurt workers who lose jobs through no fault of their own, contrasted this with a report finding the government could gain $8.4 billion a year if top 200 companies paid the full corporate tax rate, and noted more than $852 million has been paid to 70,000 workers under the scheme since 2007.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: Opposed the Fair Entitlements Guarantee Amendment Bill 2014, said more than $260 million had been paid to over 16,000 workers under the scheme and its predecessor between 2001 and 2013, recalled the 2001 collapse of One.Tel which owed $600 million including entitlements to 1,400 employees, and said manufacturing workers received more than 41 per cent of total redundancy payments under the scheme.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: Argued against the Fair Entitlements Guarantee Amendment Bill, which reduces maximum redundancy pay entitlements for workers whose employers become insolvent, saying the scheme's maximum weekly wage rate of $2451.50 will now be frozen until 30 June 2018, and questioned why the government opposes support for manufacturing workers.

speeches.speaker: Jim Chalmers
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill's proposal to cap Fair Entitlements Guarantee redundancy payments at 16 weeks instead of 52 weeks, arguing that longer payments support vulnerable and older workers through retraining after redundancy and that Labor would oppose the measure.

speeches.speaker: Justine Elliot
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill's 16-week cap on redundancy assistance, arguing that it would unfairly affect older and automotive workers, contradict prior assurances about entitlements, and compound the termination of the Automotive Transformation Scheme, including $200 million in cuts over the next two years.

speeches.speaker: Joanne Ryan
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill's proposal to cap redundancy payments at 16 weeks, arguing that it would particularly harm older and automotive workers who may lose employment and would reduce support while the government provided insufficient assistance for job creation in Melbourne's west.

speeches.speaker: Cathy McGowan
speeches.brief: Reported that 59 Bruck Textile Technologies workers in Wangaratta lost their jobs on 11 July and received most outstanding entitlements through the Fair Entitlements Guarantee within six weeks, then asked the government to ensure full payments, strengthen company oversight and make the scheme a last resort.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Opposed the Fair Entitlements Guarantee Amendment Bill, explaining the current scheme provides up to 13 weeks of unpaid wages and entitlements plus up to four weeks' redundancy pay per year of service, which this bill would cap at 16 weeks total, and noted the government claims it will save $618.5 million over eight years by terminating the Automotive Transformation Scheme from January 2018.

speeches.speaker: Nick Champion
speeches.brief: Opposed the Fair Entitlements Guarantee Amendment Bill's 16-week cap on redundancy pay, warning it would particularly hurt mature-age and long-serving workers in South Australia's automotive sector, which is closing by 2017, and criticised the government's plan to cut $500 million from the Automotive Transformation Scheme affecting about 10,000 workers in South Australia and 20,000 in Victoria.

speeches.speaker: Luke Hartsuyker
speeches.brief: Defended the Fair Entitlements Guarantee Amendment Bill, arguing it does not strip worker entitlements but sets the redundancy safety net at 16 weeks to align with the National Employment Standards and ensure the scheme's sustainability, with the cap applying to employer liquidations and bankruptcies occurring on or after 1 January 2015.
